summary:
Consensual same-sex conduct was decriminalised in Armenia in 2003, and no provision of Armenian law criminalises transgender identity or expression as such. The restrictive legislative route has been attempted: in 2013 the police proposed a bill criminalising "non-traditional sexual relationships" and LGBT "propaganda" directed at young people, modelled on Russian legislation; it failed to pass after Pink Armenia argued it functioned as a distraction tactic. A 2009 ILGA-Europe and COC fact-finding mission, Forced Out: LGBT People in Armenia, documented societal and institutional homophobia, harassment and violence, and the legislation then affecting LGBT people; the pattern it described is visible in later reporting.

Legal gender recognition has operated as an administrative practice since 2006 and requires surgery. There is no recognition of non-binary identities, and gender-affirming care is restricted. A trans visitor should expect that a change of legal marker is not available on self-declaration and that access to hormone or surgical care in Armenia is limited.

Marriage is not open to a trans visitor whose relationship would be locally classed as same-sex, or read as same-sex under birth-sex status; Armenian law bars marriage between persons of the same sex and provides no equivalent recognition. No discrimination protection exists on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and an anti-discrimination bill tabled in 2018 did not pass. Hate-crime protection covering bias-motivated violence has been characterised as ambiguous since 2022.

Pink Human Rights Defender NGO's 2024 annual report documents discrimination, torture and inhuman or degrading treatment, including sexual violence, domestic violence and extortion, directed at LGBT people in Armenia, along with violations of private and family life, of education and work rights, and hate speech. Public acceptance is low: Equaldex records a public-opinion acceptance score of 5 out of 100.

Violence against LGBT people has drawn a slow or absent state response. In May 2012 a neo-Nazi arson attack on the gay-friendly DIY bar in Yerevan involved a Molotov cocktail and a fire; police took 12 hours to respond, and two suspects were later detained on the basis of CCTV footage. In April 2019 Lilit Martirosyan, Armenia's first registered transgender woman, became the first transgender person to address the National Assembly; she received death threats, including from members of parliament who called for her to be burned alive. In February 2020 a nationalist party member burned incense over the same lectern, denouncing her speech as a desecration.
tangentialFactors:
Regional comparison data covers Armenia alongside Azerbaijan and Georgia, but the inventory supplies trans-specific findings for Armenia only; no equivalent detail for the other two jurisdictions is available here. The 2013 bill was drafted on the model of Russian legislation, an import of a restrictive framework from a neighbouring jurisdiction.

Restrictions on LGBT public expression and assembly have been documented. In 2017 the organisers of the Yerevan International Film Festival cancelled the screening of two LGBT-themed films after negative public reaction. In November 2018 a Christian LGBT group cancelled planned forums and events, citing constant threats and organised intimidation from political and religious leaders and what it described as insufficient police readiness to protect them.
localsOnly:
Attitudes among the resident population are hostile. A 2012 study found that 55% of Armenians would end a relationship with a friend or relative who came out, and 70% find LGBT people "strange".

In 2014 the newspaper Iravunk published a list of dozens of Armenian LGBT Facebook accounts, describing them as "zombies". The Court of Appeals ruled that the newspaper had not offended anyone and ordered the plaintiffs to pay 50,000 dram, about US$120, to the newspaper.

Pink Armenia's 2024 report includes a chapter on pressure brought against a transgender individual in Armenia over participation in a beauty pageant.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no general homicide rate or per-capita baseline for Armenia, so the trans-specific violence documented by Pink Armenia and the 2012 arson attack cannot be compared against a background rate. The counts are raw, and the sources describe underreporting; no magnitude should be read from them.

Whether the surgical requirement for legal gender recognition is applied to foreign nationals, and what documentation a trans visitor would need to change or match a marker, is not sourced. Whether Armenia's hate-crime provisions have produced any prosecution is unresolved in the inventory. The 2009 ILGA-Europe and COC report is dated, and the inventory does not establish which of its findings on institutional homophobia persist beyond what the 2024 Pink Armenia report documents.
